stem: Which conclusion is appropriately supported by this study design?
stimulus: A wellness magazine reports that people who meditate at least 20 minutes per day have lower blood pressure on average than people who do not meditate, based on a survey of 500 adults who volunteered to report their meditation habits and blood pressure.

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is an association between meditation habits and blood pressure in this sample, but causation cannot be concluded because participants were not randomly assigned to meditate or not.
choices.rationale: This was an observational, voluntary-response study with no random assignment of the explanatory variable, so an association can be described but a causal claim is not supported.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meditating for 20 minutes a day causes lower blood pressure.
choices.rationale: This draws a causal conclusion from an observational study with no random assignment, which cannot rule out confounding variables.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the sample size is large (500 people), causation can be concluded even without random assignment.
choices.rationale: A large sample size reduces sampling variability but does nothing to address confounding; only random assignment supports causal claims.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No conclusion can be drawn because the study did not use a randomized experiment.
choices.rationale: This overcorrects -- observational studies can still support conclusions about association, just not causation.

stem: Why is it inappropriate to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of p-hat in this situation?
stimulus: A quality control engineer wants to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of defective items in a random sample of size n = 40 from a manufacturing process where the true defect rate is p = 0.03.

choices.label: A
choices.text: np = 40(0.03) = 1.2, which is less than 10, so the success-failure condition is not met and the sampling distribution of p-hat would be skewed, not approximately normal.
choices.rationale: The success-failure condition requires both np and n(1-p) to be at least 10 (a common threshold); here np = 1.2, which fails the condition, so the normal approximation is not justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample size 40 is too small to ever use a normal approximation, regardless of p.
choices.rationale: Appropriateness depends on np and n(1-p), not on the sample size n alone; a sample of 40 could be adequate for a different value of p.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population defect rate p = 0.03 is a parameter, not a statistic, so the normal approximation does not apply to parameters.
choices.rationale: This confuses the parameter/statistic distinction with the actual condition being checked; the success-failure condition uses p to check np and n(1-p), regardless of p being a parameter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random sampling was not used, so no approximation is valid.
choices.rationale: The stimulus states the sample is random; this introduces an assumption violation that isn't actually present in the scenario.

stimulus: A data set has 12 values with mean 40. One value is changed from 18 to 30.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases by 12.
choices.rationale: That is the change in one data value, not the change in the mean.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It does not change.
choices.rationale: Changing a data value changes the mean unless the change is zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases by 0.5.
choices.rationale: This divides by the wrong number of values.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases by 1.0, because the total sum increases by 12 and the data set has 12 values.
choices.rationale: Changing one value by +12 raises the mean by 12/12 = 1.

stem: What is the upper fence for possible outliers?
stimulus: For a data set, Q1 = 18 and Q3 = 30.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses 1.0(IQR) instead of 1.5(IQR).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This mistakenly starts from Q1 instead of Q3: Q1 + 1.5(IQR) = 18 + 1.5(12) = 18 + 18 = 36.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This doubles Q3 instead of adding 1.5×IQR to it: 2 × Q3 = 2(30) = 60.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: IQR = 12, so the upper fence is Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 30 + 18 = 48.

stem: Why might stratified sampling be better than a simple random sample?
stimulus: A school has freshmen, sophomores, juniors, and seniors in different proportions.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It ensures each grade level is represented in the sample.
choices.rationale: Stratified sampling can improve representativeness when important subgroups need guaranteed representation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guarantees no bias under any circumstance.
choices.rationale: No sampling method guarantees zero bias.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It always requires fewer people than any other method.
choices.rationale: Sample size depends on the precision desired, not just the method.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes the need for random selection.
choices.rationale: Strata are typically sampled randomly within each group.

stem: What does random assignment help with most?
stimulus: A school randomly assigns students to a new tutoring program or the old program.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Guaranteeing a perfectly equal sample size in every subgroup.
choices.rationale: Random assignment does not guarantee equal subgroup sizes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminating all measurement error.
choices.rationale: Random assignment does not fix measurement problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making the study automatically double blind.
choices.rationale: Blinding is separate from random assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Balancing lurking variables between the groups so a causal comparison is more credible.
choices.rationale: Random assignment helps create comparable groups and supports causal inference.

stimulus: In a class of 40 students, 10 are athletes, and 4 of those athletes are on the honor roll.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Conditional probability uses the athlete group as the denominator.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the whole class instead of only the athletes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is P(athlete), not the conditional probability.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This incorrectly uses the number of athletes NOT on the honor roll (10 − 4 = 6) as the denominator instead of all 10 athletes: 4/6 ≈ 0.67.

stem: What is the probability that it does not rain?
stimulus: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.25.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Use the complement: 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This repeats the original probability instead of its complement.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is not the complement of 0.25.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This does not sum with 0.25 to 1.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Use the addition rule: P(A or B) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.9.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This subtracts too much or omits one event.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This adds the probabilities without correcting for overlap.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is only the intersection.

stimulus: A new estimator consistently misses the true value by a large amount, even with large samples.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only variability
choices.rationale: Large random scatter is not the only issue when the estimator is consistently off target.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normality
choices.rationale: Normality is not the central issue described here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Independence
choices.rationale: The question is about systematic error, not dependence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bias
choices.rationale: If an estimator is systematically off target, the estimator is biased.

stimulus: A survey of 200 people finds 118 support a policy. The question is whether support exceeds 50%.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Null and alternative are reversed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The claim is that support exceeds 50%, so this is a right-tailed test for a proportion.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses the wrong parameter symbol.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Proportions are not counts.

stimulus: A binomial setting has n = 5 and p = 0.5.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: That is the probability of a single success, not zero successes in five trials.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is not the correct binomial calculation for zero successes.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: That is the trial count, not a probability.

stem: Which study is most likely to have lower power?
stimulus: Two studies test the same claim, but one uses a more stringent significance level and a smaller sample size.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study with the smaller sample size and more stringent α.
choices.rationale: Lower α and smaller n both tend to reduce power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size and more stringent α.
choices.rationale: Larger n increases power, all else equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size and larger α.
choices.rationale: Larger α increases power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both studies must have the same power.
choices.rationale: Power depends on n and α, so they need not match.
